r: SPA 1000 builds basic conversational Spanish for personal travel: ordering food, asking directions, exchanging pleasantries with strangers abroad. Task-exposure research names translators and interpreters among the most-exposed occupations, and phone-based real-time translation for tourism is already widely deployed, which pushes the underlying task's automatability upward even at this horizon. Yet the graded competence is live, embodied speech production in front of another person in the moment, not a text artifact a model hands back afterward, and that keeps the course itself outside the fully-automated band. Consequence of error is low here, so verification burden is not the binding constraint; embodiment is. The course carries no general-studies designation and sits outside any prerequisite chain, so no institutional lock protects it either. At 24 months, the combination of embodied live delivery and uneven adoption of travel-translation tools in casual encounters keeps the rating Low.

By 2031, real-time speech translation for casual travel exchanges will plausibly be excellent and near-ubiquitous on ordinary phones, materially eroding the instrumental case for a dedicated course teaching the same phrases a device now supplies instantly. Observed-usage data already shows writing and translation-adjacent tasks prominent in everyday AI use, and that diffusion should only widen by this horizon. What is not automated is the traveler's own capacity for spontaneous, embodied spoken exchange when a device is unavailable, awkward, or simply slower than speaking. With no general-studies mandate or prerequisite role to cap the erosion, the rating rises to Medium, tracking the base automatability increase directly rather than being held down by institutional lock-in. The hedge is genuine: this is a course type where reasonable analysts could argue for faster erosion given how mature travel-translation apps already are.

A decade out, seamless real-time translation for tourism-level exchanges is a reasonable central-case expectation, and the instrumental rationale for learning conversational Spanish specifically to navigate travel logistics is substantially eroded — one of the more exposed course types in this batch precisely because it lacks any institutional anchor. What persists is the residual value of a traveler being able to speak directly, without mediation, in real time, which embodiment protects from full automation even under aggressive capability assumptions. The rating holds at Medium rather than rising to High because that embodied, unmediated-speech residue is real, not because any accreditation or general-studies requirement intervenes. The uncertainty is wide: this is a course whose enrollment rationale could weaken considerably as consumer translation tools mature, even though the specific rating stops short of High.
SPA 1000.d: This course is designed for the student who wants to acquire a basic knowledge of conversational Spanish for personal travel.

r: SPA 1002 teaches basic conversational Spanish for law-enforcement encounters: field communication with Spanish-speaking community members during stops, interviews, and routine calls. The underlying language task sits in the same highly-exposed translation category task-exposure research flags for translators and interpreters generally, but deployment of AI-mediated language tools inside live, safety-relevant public-safety encounters lags well behind that raw capability, and diffusion data shows adoption of AI tools across firms and institutions remains uneven. The verification burden is high: a mistranslated instruction or misread response in a law-enforcement encounter carries real safety, legal, and civil-rights consequences, and the failure is often non-obvious in the moment. No general-studies designation or broad prerequisite chain constrains the course institutionally, but the safety-critical stakes alone justify holding the rating Low at 24 months.

By 2031, AI translation earpieces and apps will be more capable and somewhat more present in public-safety settings, narrowing the raw exposure gap. But the jagged-frontier evidence is directly on point: officers relying on AI translation outside its reliable range risk acting on mistranslated, high-stakes information with mis-calibrated confidence in the output, and that verification burden keeps a human who actually speaks the language necessary in the field. Institutionally the course still carries no general-studies lock, so nothing structurally protects it beyond the task's own risk profile. The rating stays Low at five years because the dampening effect of high verification burden persists even as base automatability rises — this is a case where capability growth alone does not translate into reduced instrumental need, given what a wrong translation could cost in this context.

A decade out, AI-mediated field translation will likely be considerably more capable and more normalized in law-enforcement workflows, and the base task exposure climbs enough to move the rating to Medium. Even so, the safety-critical, adversarial nature of public-safety encounters — where a mistranslated command or misunderstood response can escalate a situation — keeps meaningful verification burden in place, which is why the rating does not rise further despite the capability trajectory. No institutional mandate intervenes either way; the constraint here is entirely about error cost rather than accreditation. The honest hedge is that this is a genuinely contested case: agencies eager to cut costs could push AI-mediated communication into routine encounters faster than the safety case warrants, which would argue for a higher rating than the central case used here.
SPA 1002.d: This course is designed for the student who wants to acquire a basic knowledge of conversational Spanish for the law- enforcement professions.

A decade out, the trajectory mirrors SPA 1002: broader deployment of AI-mediated field translation plausibly lifts the rating to Medium as base automatability rises, but the safety-critical, adversarial character of law-enforcement encounters keeps genuine verification burden in place, preventing further erosion. Nothing about being the second course in the sequence changes that calculus — the applied task and its stakes are the same, only the vocabulary and situational range are more advanced and arguably harder to hand off safely to a tool. No accreditation or general-studies mandate bears on the course either way. The uncertainty is meaningful: how fast public-safety agencies actually adopt AI-mediated communication for routine encounters, versus reserving it deliberately for lower-stakes administrative contact and keeping trained officers for anything adversarial, will determine whether this central-case Medium proves conservative or generous by 2036.
SPA 1003.d: This course is a continuation of SPA 1002 and is designed for the student who wants to acquire a basic knowledge of conversational Spanish for the law-enforcement professions.

SPA 1004.d: This course is designed for the student who wants to acquire a basic knowledge of conversational Spanish for the medical professions.

SPA 1005.d: This course is a continuation of SPA 1004 and is designed for the student who wants to acquire a basic knowledge of conversational Spanish for the medical professions.

The rating holds Low at five years, with the hedge that if schools increasingly conduct even sensitive conversations through AI-mediated channels rather than face-to-face, this course type could erode faster than the central case here assumes.

A decade out, base automatability of school-communication language tasks climbs enough that the rating rises to Medium, reflecting how much of routine parent and student communication AI-mediated tools will plausibly handle by 2036. The genuine uncertainty is how much of school-family communication migrates to asynchronous, AI-translated channels versus remaining live and in-person; that balance, more than raw translation capability alone, will determine whether this rating undershoots or overshoots the actual 2036 picture for school personnel.
SPA 1006.d: This course is designed for the student who wants to acquire a basic knowledge of conversational Spanish for the school environment.

SPA 1007.d: This course is a continuation of SPA 1006 and is designed for the student who wants to acquire a basic knowledge of conversational Spanish for the school environment.

r: Culturas Vivas is taught in English and asks students to analyze cultural artifacts — short stories, film, comics, music, architecture, cuisine, sport — across Spanish-speaking Latin America, Spain, and the United States, using an interdisciplinary and gender-inclusive lens to counter stereotyping and Hispanophobia. This is a written-analysis and critical-thinking task, not live translation or oral performance, so it sits closer to the writing-and-analysis band task-exposure research treats as more exposed than embodied work, though the course's critical-thinking and interdisciplinary framing pulls against full automatability. At 24 months the instrumental need to build the student's own interpretive and cultural literacy is intact; AI can summarize a film, but the course's purpose is the learner's own critical analysis.

What is not substituted is the student's own cultivated capacity to read cultural artifacts critically and to evaluate AI-generated analysis for accuracy and bias — an increasingly relevant skill given the course's explicit focus on countering stereotyped representation, where a model trained on biased source material could itself reproduce the very stereotypes the course critiques. The GT-Pathways-equivalent general-studies mandate caps the erosion at Medium regardless of how automatable the writing task becomes, holding the course in the transfer core across a catalog cycle.

The rating holds Medium, capped by the institutional mandate rather than by task characteristics alone. The uncertainty concerns how the writing-heavy assessments are restructured under ubiquitous AI, not whether the general-education requirement and its interpretive-literacy goal persist.
SPA 1009.d: In this course taught in English, students explore the vibrant Spanish-speaking cultures of Latin America, Spain, and the United States through an overview of history, geography, literatures, and artistic expressions with a focus on contemporary issues. Students analyze a variety of cultural artifacts, such as short stories, comics, animations, films, musical genres, architecture, cuisines, and sports. Through an interdisciplinary approach including gender perspectives, this course intends to go beyond the underrepresentation and the stereotypical characterization of Hispanic individuals on television, in films, and the news, as well as recent forms of Hispanophobia in the United States. For an even richer experience, students are encouraged to take simultaneously a course in Spanish. (If the student has already taken classes of Spanish or speak Spanish at home, he/she/they contact an advisor at the department of World Languages to be placed in the appropriate level).
